prompt: Which edge-weight assumption guarantees correctness of standard Dijkstra’s algorithm on every finite directed graph, using permanent finalization when a vertex is extracted?

answers.explanation: With nonnegative weights, extending a path cannot lower its weight. This makes it safe to finalize the unsettled vertex with smallest tentative distance.
Negative edges can invalidate an already finalized distance.

answers.text: The graph has at least one positive edge.
answers.explanation: One positive edge gives no guarantee about the remaining edges.
Degrees do not make the greedy distance invariant valid.

answers.text: The sum of all edge weights is nonnegative.
answers.explanation: A nonnegative total does not rule out a negative edge that breaks finalization.
This suffices for finite shortest-path distances, but standard Dijkstra can still fail with a negative edge.

answers.text: Every edge weight is an integer.
answers.explanation: Negative integers can break the algorithm just as negative real weights can.

answers.text: Every directed cycle has strictly positive total weight.
answers.explanation: Even an acyclic graph with a negative edge can break permanent finalization.

answers.text: All edges leaving the source are nonnegative.
answers.explanation: A later negative edge can still produce a shorter path to an already finalized vertex.

answers.text: There is at most one negative edge.
answers.explanation: A single negative edge is enough to defeat the correctness guarantee.
